claims.text: A free-energy-based computational sampling approach can guide pulsed energy deposition to form three-dimensional noble-metal high-entropy-alloy nanoframeworks.
Controlled cooling during pulsed energy deposition will produce precise atomic arrangements in the NM-HEA nanoframework.
The proposed process will preserve noble-metal compositional diversity.
The resulting nanoframework will have enhanced catalytic performance.
The initial material is a homogeneous, non-structured or amorphous mixture of noble metals pre-alloyed or co-deposited as nanoparticles.
Free-energy-based computational sampling can identify optimal pulsed-energy profiles and cooling rates for the synthesis.
The computed energy and cooling parameters can be implemented through a pulsed energy deposition technique such as pulsed laser deposition.
Tailored pulse energy and cooling under a controlled atmosphere will kinetically trap metastable three-dimensional configurations.
Kinetic trapping at locally controlled supersaturation sites will produce interconnected three-dimensional frameworks.
Modulated pulsed energy deposition creates specific nucleation sites.
Modulated pulsed energy deposition controls atomic diffusion rates.
Tailored energy input and rapid cooling limit phase separation.
Limiting phase separation promotes uniform three-dimensional nanostructures with precise atomic arrangements.
The proposed method will yield greater uniformity, atomic precision, and three-dimensional connectivity than conventional high-temperature or solution-based methods.
Conventional high-temperature melting or solution-based alloying typically produces less-controlled nanostructures lacking interconnected frameworks and atomic-scale control.
The approach is limited to NM-HEA systems for which energy modulation is feasible and compositions remain near a free-energy-model optimum.
The exact pulse-energy profile, cooling rate, and local supersaturation parameters have not been determined.
Long-term structural stability under catalytic operating conditions is uncertain.
Microscopy, XRD, BET surface-area measurements, and catalytic testing can distinguish the proposed product from a composition-matched conventional control.
